claim: TRACT is based on ligand-induced intramembrane proteolysis to reveal monosynaptic connections arising from genetically labeled neurons of interest.
source: We describe a technique called TRACT (TRAnsneuronal Control of Transcription) based on ligand-induced intramembrane proteolysis to reveal monosynaptic connections arising from genetically labeled neurons of interest.
evidence: The abstract directly states the technical basis and purpose of TRACT.

claim: In TRACT, neurons expressing an artificial ligand ('donor' neurons) bind to and activate a genetically-engineered artificial receptor on their synaptic partners ('receiver' neurons).
source: In this strategy, neurons expressing an artificial ligand ('donor' neurons) bind to and activate a genetically-engineered artificial receptor on their synaptic partners ('receiver' neurons).
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the mechanism of TRACT.

claim: Upon ligand-receptor binding at synapses, the receptor is cleaved in its transmembrane domain and releases a protein fragment that activates transcription in the synaptic partners.
source: Upon ligand-receptor binding at synapses the receptor is cleaved in its transmembrane domain and releases a protein fragment that activates transcription in the synaptic partners.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the molecular mechanism following ligand-receptor binding.

claim: Using TRACT in Drosophila, the connectivity between olfactory receptor neurons and their postsynaptic targets has been confirmed.
source: Using TRACT in Drosophila we have confirmed the connectivity between olfactory receptor neurons and their postsynaptic targets, and have discovered potential new connections between neurons in the circadian circuit.
evidence: The abstract states that TRACT confirmed known connectivity in the olfactory system.

claim: Using TRACT in Drosophila, potential new connections between neurons in the circadian circuit have been discovered.
source: Using TRACT in Drosophila we have confirmed the connectivity between olfactory receptor neurons and their postsynaptic targets, and have discovered potential new connections between neurons in the circadian circuit.
evidence: The abstract states that TRACT discovered new connections in the circadian circuit.

claim: Comprehensively mapping the connectivity of diverse neural circuits across many brain regions and many organisms is a major goal of modern neuroscience.
source: Comprehensively mapping the connectivity of diverse neural circuits across many brain regions and many organisms is a major goal of modern neuroscience (Denk et al., 2012; Bargmann and Marder, 2013; Swanson and Lichtman, 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references supporting this as a major goal of neuroscience.

claim: Aberrant neuronal wiring may be the cause of several neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: In addition, recent research indicates that aberrant neuronal wiring may be the cause of several neurodevelopmental disorders (Peça and Feng, 2012; Rubinov and Bullmore, 2013; Mevel and Fransson, 2016), further emphasizing the importance of identifying the wiring diagrams of brain circuits.
evidence: The introduction cites research indicating aberrant wiring causes neurodevelopmental disorders.

claim: A strategy based on ligand-induced intramembrane proteolysis can be used to monitor cell-cell interactions in the nervous system of transgenic Drosophila.
source: In a previous work, we demonstrated that a strategy based on ligand-induced intramembrane proteolysis can be used to monitor cell-cell interactions in the nervous system of transgenic Drosophila (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites previous work demonstrating this capability.

claim: In the original implementation, the ligand-induced intramembrane proteolysis system was not useful to trace neuronal circuits because it revealed all forms of cell-cell contact, including non-synaptic contacts.
source: However, in its original implementation, the system was not useful to trace neuronal circuits because it revealed all forms of cell-cell contact, including non-synaptic contacts.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states the limitation of the original system.

claim: To allow the strategy to trace neuronal circuits, it is necessary to ensure that the interaction of ligand and receptor occurs exclusively across synapses.
source: To allow this strategy to trace neuronal circuits it is necessary to ensure that the interaction of ligand and receptor occurs exclusively across synapses.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states the requirement for synaptic specificity.

claim: The ligand was engineered to be selectively located at the presynaptic cleft to prevent activation of the system between neurons that had non-synaptic cell-cell contacts.
source: To prevent activation of the system between neurons that had non-synaptic cell-cell contacts, we engineered the ligand so that it would be selectively located at the presynaptic cleft (Südhof, 2012; Van Vactor and Sigrist, 2017).
evidence: The introduction explicitly describes the engineering approach to achieve synaptic specificity.

claim: The Drosophila antennal lobe is an olfactory center with well-understood connectivity established by light and electron microscopy, and electrophysiological methods.
source: To validate that the optimized ligands revealed neurons specifically connected by synapses, we tested the system on the Drosophila antennal lobe, an olfactory center with well-understood connectivity established by light and electron microscopy, and electrophysiological methods (Grabe et al., 2016; Stocker et al., 1990; Wilson, 2013; Rybak et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references establishing the antennal lobe connectivity.

claim: Adding domains from the synaptic proteins synaptobrevin (nSyb) or syndecan (sdc) was sufficient to achieve reliable synaptic tracing in the antennal lobe.
source: We observed that adding domains from the synaptic proteins synaptobrevin (nSyb) or syndecan (sdc) was sufficient to achieve reliable synaptic tracing in the antennal lobe.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states the result of adding these domains.

claim: TRACT was used to investigate the connectivity of the Drosophila circadian system.
source: In addition, we used TRACT to investigate the connectivity of the Drosophila circadian system, a compact brain circuit with a small number of neurons (Dubowy and Sehgal, 2017; Nitabach and Taghert, 2008), and discovered new candidate postsynaptic targets for the PDF neurons of the circadian system in the central brain, some of which that express the circadian-related gene, per.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states TRACT was used to investigate circadian connectivity.

claim: New candidate postsynaptic targets for the PDF neurons of the circadian system in the central brain were discovered, some of which express the circadian-related gene, per.
source: In addition, we used TRACT to investigate the connectivity of the Drosophila circadian system, a compact brain circuit with a small number of neurons (Dubowy and Sehgal, 2017; Nitabach and Taghert, 2008), and discovered new candidate postsynaptic targets for the PDF neurons of the circadian system in the central brain, some of which that express the circadian-related gene, per.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states the discovery of new candidate targets.

claim: The original artificial ligand CD19mch contains the extracellular and transmembrane domains of the mouse lymphocyte antigen CD19 fused to the red fluorescent protein mCherry in its intracellular domain.
source: In its original implementation, we used a ligand called CD19mch that contains the extracellular and transmembrane domains (ECD and TMD) of the mouse lymphocyte antigen CD19 (Fujimoto et al., 1998) fused to the red fluorescent protein mCherry in its intracellular domain (ICD).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the composition of the original ligand.

claim: The original artificial receptor SNTG4 contains the ECD from a single chain antibody (ID3) that recognizes mouse CD19, the Notch regulatory region (NRR) and the TMD from Drosophila Notch, and esn, a simplified version of the yeast transcriptional activator Gal4.
source: The original artificial receptor is called SNTG4 and contains the following domains (in N-to-C terminal order): (i) the ECD from a single chain antibody (ID3) that recognizes mouse CD19 (Kochenderfer et al., 2009), (ii) the Notch regulatory region (NRR) and the TMD from Drosophila Notch (spanning from EGF repeat 36 until the ICD) (Kovall et al., 2017), and (iii) esn, a simplified version of the yeast transcriptional activator Gal4 (Figure 1a) (Sprinzak et al., 2010).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the composition of the original receptor.

claim: Expression of the ligand and receptor in neurons leads to the distribution of these two proteins uniformly throughout the membrane, including cell body, dendrite branches, and axons.
source: In this configuration, expression of the ligand and receptor in neurons leads to the distribution of these two proteins uniformly throughout the membrane, including cell body, dendrite branches, and axons.
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the distribution pattern of the original ligand and receptor.

claim: A UAS-GFP reporter transgene was included to detect the activation of the receptor upon interaction with its ligand in vivo in Drosophila.
source: To detect the activation of the receptor upon interaction with its ligand in vivo in Drosophila, we included a UAS-GFP reporter transgene, which expresses GFP in response to Gal4 activity (Brand and Perrimon, 1993).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the reporter system used.

claim: The antennal lobe is the second-order olfactory processing area in the Drosophila brain that receives direct input from the primary olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs).
source: To test whether the expression of the ligand in donor neurons could reveal the subset of receiver neurons that receive synaptic input from them, we focused on the antennal lobe, the second-order olfactory processing area in the Drosophila brain that receives direct input from the primary olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) (Figure 2a, Wilson, 2013; Laissue and Vosshall, 2008).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the antennal lobe and cites references.

claim: Synapses in the antennal lobe are organized into discrete compartments, called glomeruli, and each glomerulus corresponds to a distinct ORN class.
source: Synapses in the antennal lobe are organized into discrete compartments, called glomeruli, and each glomerulus corresponds to a distinct ORN class (defined by the odorant receptor it expresses) (Berck et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the organization of the antennal lobe and cites a reference.

claim: All ORNs of a specific class project their axons to a common glomerulus.
source: All ORNs of a specific class project their axons to a common glomerulus (Vosshall et al., 1999; Fishilevich and Vosshall, 2005; Couto et al., 2005).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes ORN projection patterns and cites references.

claim: The vast majority of PNs are uniglomerular PNs (uniPNs), and each of these uniPNs have dendrites that branch into single glomeruli where they receive direct synaptic input from a single class of ORNs.
source: The vast majority of PNs are uniglomerular PNs (uniPNs) (Figure 2b), and each of these uniPNs have dendrites that branch into single glomeruli where they receive direct synaptic input from a single class of ORNs.
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes uniPN anatomy and connectivity.

claim: Axonal output from uniPNs projects to two major third-order olfactory areas, the mushroom body and the lateral horn, via the medial antennal lobe tract (mALT).
source: Axonal output from uniPNs projects to two major third-order olfactory areas, the mushroom body and the lateral horn, via the medial antennal lobe tract (mALT, formerly iACT) (Ito et al., 2014), (Figure 2a).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes uniPN projection patterns and cites a reference.

claim: Multiglomerular PNs (multiPNs) have dendritic arbors which pool input across multiple glomeruli in the antennal lobe, and send their output to the lateral horn only via the mediolateral ALT (mlALT).
source: In addition, a smaller subset of PNs, multiglomerular PNs (multiPNs) (Figure 2c) (Stocker et al., 1990; Parnas et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2013), have dendritic arbors which pool input across multiple glomeruli in the antennal lobe, and send their output to the lateral horn only via the mediolateral ALT (mlALT, formerly the mACT) (Figure 2a) (Tanaka et al., 2012).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes multiPN anatomy and connectivity and cites references.

claim: Local neurons (LNs) send and receive synaptic input from both ORNs and PNs, densely interconnecting the glomeruli.
source: Finally, a large set of local neurons (LNs) send and receive synaptic input from both ORNs and PNs, densely interconnecting the glomeruli (Figure 2d) (Chou et al., 2010; Hong and Wilson, 2015; Seki et al., 2010).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes LN connectivity and cites references.

claim: Expression of the original TRACT ligand and receptor (without any domains that would localize them to synaptic sites) in neurons failed to reveal any synaptic connections in the antennal lobe.
source: Expression of the original TRACT ligand and receptor (without any domains that would localize them to synaptic sites) in neurons failed to reveal any synaptic connections in the antennal lobe.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the failure of the original system.

claim: When the CD19mch ligand is expressed in the majority of ORNs using the Orco-lexA driver and the SNTG4 receptor is expressed from the elav enhancer, no GFP induction was observed in the antennal lobe.
source: For instance, when the CD19mch ligand is expressed in the majority of ORNs using the Orco-lexA driver (Stocker et al., 1997) and the SNTG4 receptor is expressed from the elav enhancer (Yao and White, 1994), we predicted labeling of both PNs and LNs, the major postsynaptic targets in the antennal lobe. However, in flies carrying Orco > CD19 mch, elav-SNTG4, UAS-GFP transgenes, no GFP induction was observed in the antennal lobe (data not shown), consistent with the findings from another publication (He et al., 2017), suggesting that the system needed adjustments to detect synaptic connections.
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the negative result with the original system and cites references.

claim: In flies carrying orco>nSybCD19 or orco>CD19 sdc, nSybE-nlgSNTG4, and UAS-CD4tdGFP, GFP expression was observed in dozens of neurons in the antennal lobe.
source: To test the ability of TRACT to reveal the connectivity originating from ORNs, we generated flies carrying orco>nSybCD19 or orco>CD19 sdc, nSybE-nlgSNTG4, and UAS-CD4tdGFP. In these flies, we observed GFP expression in dozens of neurons in the antennal lobe.
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the observation of GFP expression with the modified system.

claim: Roughly half the GFP+ neurons observed with orco>nSybCD19 or orco>CD19 sdc were PNs, which can be identified by their axons projecting into the mushroom body and lateral horn.
source: Roughly half the GFP+ neurons were PNs, which can be identified by their axons projecting into the mushroom body and lateral horn, consistent with the known connectivity between ORNs and PNs (Figure 2e, top panels).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the identification of PNs among GFP+ neurons.

claim: The cell bodies of the putative PNs labeled by TRACT were located in the anterodorsal, lateral, and ventral sectors of the antennal lobe, consistent with them being PNs.
source: In addition, the cell bodies of these axon-bearing neurons were located in the anterodorsal, lateral, and ventral sectors of the antennal lobe, consistent with them being PNs.
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the location of cell bodies consistent with PN identity.

claim: Most of the putative PNs labeled by TRACT were immunopositive for CHAT, a known marker of PNs.
source: Finally, most of the putative PNs were immunopositive for CHAT, a known marker of PNs (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes CHAT immunopositivity confirming PN identity.

claim: Around half the GFP+ neurons in the antennal lobe did not have axons, were immunopositive for GABA, and their cell bodies were located dorsolateral and ventrolateral, all features consistent with them being LNs.
source: Around half the GFP+ neurons in the antennal lobe did not have axons, were immunopositive for GABA, and their cell bodies were located dorsolateral and ventrolateral, all features consistent with them being LNs (Figure 2e, top panels and Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 5) (Okada et al., 2009).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes features consistent with LN identity and cites a reference.

claim: In Drosophila, all ORNs expressing the same olfactory receptor project their axons into two bilaterally symmetric glomeruli in the antennal lobe.
source: In Drosophila, all ORNs expressing the same olfactory receptor project their axons into two bilaterally symmetric glomeruli in the antennal lobe (Grabe et al., 2016; Tanaka et al., 2012).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes ORN projection patterns and cites references.

claim: The dendrites of individual uniPNs branch into single glomeruli where they make synapses with the axons of ORNs.
source: In addition, the dendrites of individual uniPNs branch into single glomeruli where they make synapses with the axons of ORNs (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes uniPN dendritic branching and synaptic connectivity.

claim: With the nSyb::CD19 and CD19::sdc ligands, the uniPNs labeled projected their dendrites selectively into the glomeruli where the ligand was expressed.
source: We observed that with the nSyb::CD19 and CD19::sdc ligands, the uniPNs labeled projected their dendrites selectively into the glomeruli where the ligand was expressed, consistent with previous work (Figure 3) (Grabe et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the selective labeling of uniPNs and cites a reference.

claim: When the nSyb::CD19 ligand was expressed with the R17H02-LexA driver in the DA1 glomerulus, approximately 11 labeled uniPNs were observed.
source: For example, a study using photoactivatable GFP (paGFP) indicated that between 8 and 10 PNs receive input from the DA1 glomerulus (Grabe et al., 2016), and when we expressed the nSyb::CD19 ligand with the R17H02-LexA driver in the DA1 glomerulus, we observed ~11 labeled uniPNs (Figure 3a and Table 1a).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the number of labeled PNs and cites a reference.

claim: With the nSyb::CD19 ligand, one uniPN expressed GFP in each of the VA6 and VC1 glomeruli.
source: Similarly, previous work indicated that between 1–3 and 1–2 PNs receive input from the VA6 and VC1 glomeruli, respectively, and with the nSyb::CD19 ligand, we observed that one uniPN expressed GFP in each of these glomeruli (Figure 3a and Table 1a) (Grabe et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the number of labeled PNs and cites a reference.

claim: In the VA1lm glomerulus, no induction in PNs was observed with the nSyb::CD19, which may be due to the low level of the receptor expression in this glomerulus.
source: In the VA1lm glomerulus, we did not observe any induction in PNs with the nSyb::CD19, which may be due to the low level of the receptor expression in this glomerulus (Figure 3a).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the lack of induction and provides a possible explanation.

claim: When using the CD19::sdc ligand in identified glomeruli, one PN was labeled in VA6 and VC1 and approximately 12 PNs were labeled in DA1.
source: When using the CD19::sdc ligand in identified glomeruli, we observed one PN labeled in VA6 and VC1 and ~12 PNs labeled in DA1 (Figure 3b and Table 1b).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the number of labeled PNs with CD19::sdc.

claim: A single copy of CD19::sdc was sufficient to label multiPNs, while two copies of nSyb::CD19 were necessary to produce any multiPN labeling.
source: Whereas we could achieve labeling of multiPNs with a single copy of CD19::sdc (in heterozygote animals) (Figures 3b and 4b), we could only detect multiPNs when the nSyb::CD19 ligand was present in two copies (homozygote animals) (Figures 3a and 4a).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the difference in multiPN labeling between the two ligands.

claim: The amount of ligand may be a limiting factor for transneuronal labeling.
source: This observation suggests first, that the amount of ligand may be a limiting factor for transneuronal labeling, and second, that in some cases, the CD19::sdc could be more effective at revealing some synaptic partners than nSyb::CD19.
evidence: The Results section explicitly suggests ligand amount as a limiting factor based on observations.

claim: In some cases, the CD19::sdc could be more effective at revealing some synaptic partners than nSyb::CD19.
source: This observation suggests first, that the amount of ligand may be a limiting factor for transneuronal labeling, and second, that in some cases, the CD19::sdc could be more effective at revealing some synaptic partners than nSyb::CD19.
evidence: The Results section explicitly suggests CD19::sdc may be more effective in some cases.

claim: Both the nSyb::CD19 and CD19::sdc ligands selectively reveal neurons connected by synaptic contacts between ORNs and PNs.
source: These results indicate that both the nSyb::CD19 and CD19::sdc ligands selectively reveal neurons connected by synaptic contacts between ORNs and PNs, match the available data from previously published works, and confirm that TRACT can be used to perform anterograde transneuronal tracing of brain circuits in the Drosophila brain.

claim: TRACT can be used to perform anterograde transneuronal tracing of brain circuits in the Drosophila brain.
source: These results indicate that both the nSyb::CD19 and CD19::sdc ligands selectively reveal neurons connected by synaptic contacts between ORNs and PNs, match the available data from previously published works, and confirm that TRACT can be used to perform anterograde transneuronal tracing of brain circuits in the Drosophila brain.
evidence: The Results section explicitly confirms TRACT's capability for anterograde tracing.

claim: The Drosophila circadian circuit consists of a relatively low number of neurons (around 150).
source: There are two key advantages of the circadian circuit to test the usefulness of the TRACT system: (i) it consists of a relatively low number of neurons (around 150), and (ii) the function and anatomy of many of those neurons are known in some detail, although their connectivity is not fully understood (Beckwith and Ceriani, 2015; Peschel and Helfrich-Förster, 2011; Shafer et al., 2006).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the number of neurons in the circadian circuit and cites references.

claim: The function and anatomy of many neurons in the circadian circuit are known in some detail, although their connectivity is not fully understood.
source: There are two key advantages of the circadian circuit to test the usefulness of the TRACT system: (i) it consists of a relatively low number of neurons (around 150), and (ii) the function and anatomy of many of those neurons are known in some detail, although their connectivity is not fully understood (Beckwith and Ceriani, 2015; Peschel and Helfrich-Förster, 2011; Shafer et al., 2006).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the state of knowledge about the circadian circuit and cites references.

claim: There are two types of PDF neurons in the Drosophila brain: s-LNv neurons and l-LNv neurons.
source: There are two types of PDF neurons in the Drosophila brain: (i) s-LNv neurons, which project their axons into the dorsal regions of the central brain, and (ii) l-LNv neurons, which have large dendrites that branch in the optic lobe, and an axon that projects to the contralateral optic lobe (Figure 5a).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the two types of PDF neurons.

claim: s-LNv neurons project their axons into the dorsal regions of the central brain.
source: There are two types of PDF neurons in the Drosophila brain: (i) s-LNv neurons, which project their axons into the dorsal regions of the central brain, and (ii) l-LNv neurons, which have large dendrites that branch in the optic lobe, and an axon that projects to the contralateral optic lobe (Figure 5a).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes s-LNv projection patterns.

claim: l-LNv neurons have large dendrites that branch in the optic lobe, and an axon that projects to the contralateral optic lobe.
source: There are two types of PDF neurons in the Drosophila brain: (i) s-LNv neurons, which project their axons into the dorsal regions of the central brain, and (ii) l-LNv neurons, which have large dendrites that branch in the optic lobe, and an axon that projects to the contralateral optic lobe (Figure 5a).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes l-LNv anatomy.

source: Previous works using GRASP suggested that s-LNv neurons were connected to the DN1p (Cavanaugh et al., 2014; Seluzicki et al., 2014) and DN2 neurons (Tang et al., 2017) in the adult fly.

source: In addition, it has been reported that s-LNv neurons make weak connections with LNd neurons that vary throughout the day (Gorostiza et al., 2014).

source: In the flies carrying pdf>nSyb::CD19, nSybE-nlgSNTG4 and UAS-CD4::tdGFP, we observed several neurons located in the central brain that expressed GFP (Figures 5b and 6 and Table 1c).

source: Consistent with a previous work (Tang et al., 2017) indicating the s-LNvs make synaptic contacts with DN2 neurons, we performed immunocytochemistry using an antibody against the PER protein and observed GFP+, PER+ neurons in the DN2 cluster in 10 out of 18 hemispheres (Figures 5b and 6b, and Table 1c).

source: In our experiments, in seven hemispheres we observed one GFP+, PER+ DN2 neuron, and in three hemispheres we observed two GFP+, PER+ DN2 neurons (Figures 5b and 6b, and Table 1c).

source: In contrast to previous works, we did not observe any GFP+ cells in the DN1 cluster but we observed several GFP+ cells that were PER-, close to the DN1 cluster (Figures 5b and 6a) (Cavanaugh et al., 2014) (Seluzicki et al., 2014).

claim: GFP induction was observed in some of the DN3 neurons in all the brains analyzed.

source: Finally, we observed GFP induction in some of the DN3 neurons in all the brains we analyzed (Table 1c), and we confirmed that all the GFP+ cells in DN3s were also PER+ (Figures 5b and 6b).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the PER+ status of GFP+ DN3 neurons.

source: These observations indicate that TRACT can be used to discover candidate synaptic partners in an unbiased manner. Whereas the overall pattern of transneuronal labeling observed is broadly comparable when using the sdc or nSyb ligands, in some cases there may be potential synaptic partners that may be specifically revealed by one of the ligands, and that further experiments will be required to validate these putative connections.

source: This feature is particularly advantageous for Drosophila (Bellen et al., 2010; St Johnston, 2002), mice (Anderson and Ingham, 2003; Kile and Hilton, 2005) and zebrafish (Fetcho and Liu, 1998; Patton and Zon, 2001), three model organisms of great interest to neurobiologists, with an extensive arsenal of genetic tools.
